idiom_name: servant role + capability interface + caller (or forwarding serviced objects)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: factor the shared behaviour into a servant that holds no serviced-object state; give it a minimal capability interface that the serviced classes implement (for example Movable with getPosition/setPosition); let callers pass serviced objects to the servant, or let each serviced object hold a servant and forward to it (the two published forms). Keep the servant substitutable (an object, not a global function table) and the capability interface role-shaped rather than a window into the class's state. Where the language offers a direct attachment facility - extension methods, extension functions, mixin modules, protocol extensions, free functions, extension traits - use it instead of hand-rolling the class structure; the servant object itself is only needed when the behaviour carries policy state or must be substituted.
pitfalls: Widening the capability interface so that the servant can reach further in trades the serviced class's invariants for the servant's convenience; keep the interface role-shaped.
A servant must not accumulate per-client state: per-object state belongs to the serviced objects, otherwise the servant becomes a hidden shared global.

A servant that has to test the type of its arguments (instanceof, isinstance, dynamic_cast, type-switch) is a sign that the behaviour was polymorphic and belongs in the types — migrate to Visitor or double dispatch.
A static or utility-class servant (class with static methods only) cannot be mocked, configured per scenario, or replaced at test time: always prefer an injectable instance.

When the capability interface requires a new method just to satisfy one servant, reconsider whether the behaviour belongs in the class instead — adding servant-driven accessors is a common path to anemic domain models.

Wrong move: widen the capability interface mid-flight so one servant can reach one more getter -> every implementer breaks at compile time (Oracle's 'Evolving Interfaces' documents exactly this; Java 8 default methods and C# 8 default interface members exist only to soften it) and the serviced class's encapsulation erodes one servant-driven accessor at a time -> add a second, narrower servant, pass the extra value as a parameter, or require a sub-interface that only the newly-served classes implement.

Wrong move: ship the servant as a static/utility class because it is stateless today -> the day it needs I/O, a clock, a locale or a retry policy, every call site and every test is welded to the concrete implementation and cannot substitute one -> start with an injectable instance even when it holds no fields; staticness is a decision to revisit, never a default.
